hero.badge: Radix Seal, the self-custody trust standard
hero.p: Radix Seal turns the Radix Wallet into your institution's own certificate authority. Documents are signed and encrypted entirely in the browser, files travel peer-to-peer between the parties, and proofs are anchored on a public ledger that anyone (auditor, regulator or counterparty) can verify independently, forever.
hero.security_key: Your wallet works like a security key (passkey): you prove your identity by signing a challenge, without ever exposing the key.
hero.illustration_alt: The Radix Seal insignia: an embossed seal on paper
hero.illustration_caption: The Radix Seal: an open on-ledger standard. Each user self-mints a soulbound seal NFT that acts as the insignia of their attestation collection: the on-chain equivalent of an institutional stamp, held in self-custody.
hero.metric1: Servers that ever store your files, messages or keys
hero.metric2: Of the cryptography runs client-side, in your browser
hero.metric3: Tools under one trust model: collection, sign, encrypt and chat
hero.metric4: Wallet signature is all it takes to prove control of an account

slides.p: Radix Seal turns the Radix Wallet into your institution's own certificate authority. Everything happens in the browser and proofs are anchored on a public ledger that anyone can verify independently, forever.

The certificate proves each signature without depending on this site: anyone verifies it with the original file, with no Radix account needed. And if you want, you anchor the signature as a soulbound NFT in your collection for an on-ledger record.
Content is encrypted locally and travels peer-to-peer between browsers. With ROLA + Ledger you authorize specific accounts in advance and there is a public record of who may decrypt.

capabilities.label: The toolset
capabilities.sub: Every Radix Seal tool follows the same rule: your wallet proves identity, your browser does the cryptography, and no intermediary ever holds content or keys. Available today in the Radix console.

tools.title: Your signing collection
tools.desc: Your insignia and the collection where your signatures and invitations live. It is the chain of custody that makes an on-ledger signature yours and no one else's: the collection belongs to your insignia, and your insignia can never leave your account.
points: Created for you the first time you sign or encrypt: no need to come here to start
Editable issuer identity: your organisation's name, logo and website, on everything you issue
Several collections when you need them: one to sign as an individual and another as a company, or one per company
What you have issued never moves and can never be deleted: switching only decides where the next ones are minted
One insignia can carry several collections, or each identity can have its own with its own logo

tools.title: Sign documents
tools.desc: Sign any file with your Radix Wallet. The document is hashed locally and never uploaded: only the hash is signed, proving integrity, timestamp and control of the account key.
points: Attached certificate or embedded directly inside the PDF
Visible signature page inside the PDF, readable in any viewer
Optional signature with your own X.509 certificate (PAdES), recognised by Adobe and Foxit
A trusted RFC 3161 timestamp on every signature: the date does not come from your browser
Optional on-ledger anchoring as a soulbound NFT
Multi-party signing: several signers on one certificate
Identity disclosure you control: name, email or signature only
Anyone can verify, no wallet or account needed

tools.title: Encrypt files
tools.desc: The encryption key is derived from your wallet signature via ROLA: only the account that encrypted a file can ever unlock it. Files are processed in chunks, entirely in the browser.
points: No file size limit: chunked, never uploaded
Key derived from your wallet: nothing to store or lose
Direct browser-to-browser transfer, end-to-end encrypted
Receiver decrypts only when the owner approves and signs
ROLA + Ledger mode: only accounts holding your invitation NFT can ask for the key. Without that NFT in their wallet, there is no decryption.
Resumable transfer: if the connection drops, the file continues where it stopped

tools.title: Secure chat
tools.desc: End-to-end encrypted conversations where both sides prove who they are by signing with their wallet. The session key is derived from that verified exchange: no server can read, alter or impersonate anything.
points: Both participants wallet-verified before the room opens
Messages travel peer-to-peer over an encrypted channel
Each invitation link works for a single conversation
Identity checks verified locally, in each browser
Encrypted file sending with no size limit over the same channel
Nothing leaves your browser: messages vanish when the page closes and the local copy of received files is deleted after 24 hours
Typing indicator, and the other side's wallet name above their address

encryption.label: Encryption
encryption.sub: Radix Seal locks a file to your account with a key derived from your wallet, encrypts it in your browser and shares it peer-to-peer. No server ever holds your file or your key. Here is how it works, why it fits institutions, and how it improves on current methods.

steps.title: Key from your wallet
steps.desc: The AES-256 key is derived from a deterministic ROLA signature over a per-file challenge, so only the account that encrypted the file can re-derive it. Nothing is stored: no password, no key file.

steps.title: Encrypted in your browser
steps.desc: The file is encrypted chunk by chunk with AES-256-GCM, entirely on your device. There is no size limit, and not a single byte ever reaches a server.

steps.title: Shared peer-to-peer
steps.desc: When you share it, the file travels over a direct, end-to-end encrypted channel between browsers. The receiver opens a link and it transfers browser to browser.

steps.title: On-ledger access record
steps.desc: With ROLA + Ledger, the encryptor mints a signature marking that this account encrypted the file, plus one invitation per authorized receiver, so who may decrypt is a public, verifiable record.

institutions.title: Data sovereignty
institutions.desc: Documents and keys never touch a third-party server: no data processor holding your content, no cross-border transfer to assess, and no vendor breach that can expose your files.

institutions.title: No key-management burden
institutions.desc: The key is re-derivable from the wallet your organization already controls, so there is nothing to store, rotate, escrow or lose, and no key server to secure.

institutions.title: Auditable access
institutions.desc: With ROLA + Ledger, who was authorized and who decrypted is recorded on a public ledger, verifiable years later with no vendor account and no API that may have been retired.

encryption.comparisonTitle: How it improves on current methods

comparison.title: No keys to share or leak
comparison.desc: The key is derived from your wallet and never leaves it. You never send passwords or key files over any channel, so there is no key leak, and the file itself never leaves your device, so there is no information leak either.

comparison.title: Only the encryptor can release it
comparison.desc: Only the account that encrypted the file can re-derive the key. Nobody else, not even this site, can decrypt it without that account's explicit approval, signed with its wallet.

comparison.title: Free to use
comparison.desc: Encrypting, sharing and decrypting are free. Today's tools are usually paid, with a license or a per-user or per-file subscription. Here the only possible cost is a fraction of a cent in network fees, and only if you choose the ledger record.

comparison.title: The ledger, only if you want a record
comparison.desc: Everything works locally and peer-to-peer without touching the chain. You only interact with the ledger if you want a public, verifiable record of who encrypted the file and who may decrypt it.

trust.label: The trust model
trust.sub: Traditional trust infrastructure asks you to delegate: to a SaaS vendor, to a certificate authority, to a key server. Radix Seal inverts the model: the keys stay in your wallet, the computation stays on your device, and the only shared dependency is a public, decentralized ledger.

pillars.title: Self-custody keys
pillars.desc: Identity is proven with ROLA: the wallet signs a challenge, never revealing the key. The same key management your institution already uses for assets now backs signatures, encryption and messaging.

pillars.title: Local cryptography
pillars.desc: Hashing, encryption, decryption and verification all run in the browser. Documents, messages and plaintext never leave the device: there is no upload step to secure, audit or breach.

pillars.title: Peer-to-peer transport
pillars.desc: When content must move between parties (an encrypted file, a chat message) it travels over a direct, end-to-end encrypted channel between browsers. No intermediary storage, no server in the data path.

pillars.title: Public, permanent proof
pillars.desc: Optionally, a document hash is anchored on the Radix ledger as a soulbound NFT. The proof is timestamped by consensus, immutable, and verifiable by anyone without a Radix account.

trust.standard_title: An open on-ledger standard, not a product
trust.standard_sub: Radix Seal is defined by public metadata conventions on the Radix ledger. Any wallet, explorer or third-party tool can implement it: discover a signer's attestation collection, check its insignia and verify its certificates, with no permission from us and no proprietary format in the way.

standard_points.title: Soulbound insignia
standard_points.desc: Each user self-mints a non-transferable seal NFT: it cannot be bought, sold or stolen. Each account mints its own by signing with its wallet, so holding the seal proves you control that account, and only you can use it.

standard_points.title: Attestation collections
standard_points.desc: Signatures and invitations live in per-user collections whose owner and minter is the user's own seal: a chain of custody readable on-ledger.

standard_points.title: Only hashes on-chain
standard_points.desc: The ledger stores document hashes, never documents, names or messages. Public verifiability without publishing anything confidential.

institutions.label: For institutions
institutions.sub: Banks, public administrations, law firms and healthcare providers share the same three problems: prove who signed what and when, keep confidential data confidential, and avoid betting their evidence on a vendor's survival. Radix Seal addresses all three by design.

cards.title: Audit trail by consensus
cards.desc: An anchored signature is timestamped by the network's consensus, not by a vendor's clock. Years later, an auditor or regulator verifies it against the public ledger directly, with no vendor account, no API contract and no certificate chain that may have expired in the meantime.

cards.title: Data sovereignty by architecture
cards.desc: Documents, messages and encryption keys never touch a third-party server, so there is no data processor holding your content, no cross-border transfer to assess, and no vendor breach that can expose your files. What never leaves the building cannot leak from someone else's cloud.

cards.title: No vendor lock-in
cards.desc: Radix Seal is an open standard over a public ledger with open-source tooling. Certificates are plain JSON, proofs are ordinary ledger entries, and verification needs no proprietary software. If this website disappeared tomorrow, every proof would remain verifiable.

cards.title: Procurement-friendly economics
cards.desc: No per-envelope licensing, no per-seat subscription, no infrastructure to deploy or maintain. Signing and verifying are free; anchoring a proof on-ledger costs a fraction of a cent in network fees. The trust budget goes to zero, not to a line item.

strip.label: Of verification possible without any vendor account or API
Network fee to anchor a proof on-ledger, no subscriptions
Public ledger availability: proofs outlive any vendor
Confidential bytes published: only hashes reach the ledger

comparison.label: Head to head
comparison.sub: Cloud e-signature suites, PKI with qualified certificates and PGP are today's benchmarks for signing and encrypting. Each one delegates something (custody, confidentiality or longevity) that Radix Seal keeps in your hands.

rows.saas: The vendor: signatures are applied on their servers
rows.pki: Smartcard or HSM, issued and revocable by a CA
rows.seal: Your wallet: self-custody, no issuer above you

rows.saas: The vendor's goodwill, uptime and security
rows.pki: Hierarchical CAs, single points of failure
rows.pgp: Web of trust, hard to scale beyond experts

rows.saas: Uploaded to the vendor's cloud to be signed
rows.pki: Often uploaded to portals in signing workflows
rows.pgp: Stays local, but usually sent by email
rows.seal: Never leaves the browser: only the hash is signed

rows.saas: Through the vendor's servers and storage
Requires the vendor's portal or API to exist
rows.pki: Requires CA chain plus CRL/OCSP status checks
rows.pgp: Requires key servers and fingerprint checks
rows.seal: Anyone with the file and the public ledger, no account

rows.saas: Attested by the vendor's own clock
rows.seal: Network consensus when anchored; free RFC 3161 stamp otherwise

rows.saas: As long as the vendor exists and keeps records
rows.pki: Until certificate expiry or CA revocation
rows.pgp: As long as keys are safely kept
rows.seal: As long as the public ledger exists
Open source: near-zero network fee, no subscription

rows.saas: Email, SMS or KYC verification depending on plan
rows.seal: Self-declared by the wallet; no legal binding

rows.saas: One click from the email, nothing to install
rows.pki: Card or token plus dedicated software
rows.seal: Requires the Radix Wallet and a one-time setup
Essential invite and on-ledger status flow

comparison.note: A Radix Seal signature proves the integrity of a document, its timestamp against an independent clock (network consensus, or an RFC 3161 timestamping authority), and control of the signing account, with any disclosed name self-declared by the signer's wallet. Where regulation requires an identity-verified qualified signature (such as eIDAS QES), Radix Seal complements those schemes with stronger custody, confidentiality and longevity. When idOS (decentralized identity) is implemented on Radix, a Radix Seal signature could reach legal validity, by binding the signing account to a verified identity.

explanations.custody: True self-custody: the key never leaves your wallet or your device. PGP also keeps it local; the difference is the wallet adds recovery and guided signing without managing keyrings by hand.
explanations.anchor: A public, decentralized ledger does not depend on the honesty of a company or a CA: thousands of nodes validate every transaction and anyone can read it. There is no single point to compromise or that can disappear.
explanations.confidential: The document is hashed in your browser and only that hash gets signed. The content is never transmitted to any server, so nobody (not even this site) can see it.
explanations.transfer: The direct channel runs browser to browser with end-to-end encryption. No server stores or sees the file along the way.
explanations.verify: Verification only takes the file and a read of the public ledger: no accounts, no vendor API, and no dependence on this site still existing.
explanations.timestamp: When anchored, the timestamp is fixed by network consensus and no company controls it. A signature made off the ledger carries an RFC 3161 token from a timestamping authority, at no cost and with no subscription. Either way verification holds the declared date against that independent clock and says so when they disagree.
explanations.longevity: The proof lives on a public ledger replicated by hundreds of nodes: it does not expire with a certificate or vanish if a vendor shuts down.
explanations.cost: No subscriptions or per-document pricing: just the network fee, a fraction of a cent. PGP is also free, but its operational cost in key management and training is high.
explanations.identity: Qualified PKI covers something Radix Seal does not yet: an authority validates the signer's legal identity and regulation (eIDAS QES) grants it the highest evidentiary status. Radix Seal proves control of the account, not who you legally are (once idOS lands on Radix, this gap narrows).
explanations.ease: Cloud suites have less friction for the occasional signer: a link in the email and done. Radix Seal asks for a wallet install and a one-time setup before the first signature.
explanations.workflow: Years of product give SaaS suites templates, automatic reminders and dozens of integrations. Radix Seal covers the essential invite, sign and verify flow today.

cta.sub: Sign a document, encrypt a file or open a verified conversation, right now, from your browser, with the wallet your organization already controls.

privacy.label: Privacy by design
privacy.sub: All the cryptographic work happens on your device. The only thing that touches the network is the bare minimum anyone needs to verify: the document hash and the signing accounts.

cards.title: Local hashing
cards.desc: The document is digested with Blake2b-256 in your browser, and signing means signing that hash. The content is never transmitted to any server.

cards.title: Direct browser-to-browser channel
cards.desc: When the file must reach another signer, it travels browser to browser over an end-to-end encrypted channel. No cloud in between.

cards.title: Identity under your control
cards.desc: Name or email are only included if you decide so, and they live in the certificate, not on the ledger. The chain holds only hashes and accounts.

cards.title: No accounts, no sign-up
cards.desc: No registration, email or password. Your wallet is your identity and the only key able to mint into your collection.

verifyOpen.label: Open verification
verifyOpen.sub: A Radix Seal signature does not depend on this site. The standard is a set of public metadata conventions: any tool can read the ledger and reach the same conclusion.

cards.title: Self-contained PDF
cards.desc: The signed PDF carries the certificate and the intact original document inside. One file is enough to verify the full signature.

cards.title: Public request key
cards.desc: Every signing request has a key (collection and id) that lets anyone query the ledger for who had to sign and who has signed already. When verifying, the key YOU supply outranks the one the certificate names, so the required-signer list is not chosen by whoever produced it.

cards.title: Chain of custody on-ledger
cards.desc: Each signer's collection is guarded by their non-transferable Seal: a proof of authorship read straight from the chain, trusting nobody.

verifyOpen.apiHint: Your systems can check a certificate with no browser, no wallet, no account and no API key. The endpoint never receives the document, only the certificate.
verifyOpen.apiNote: It answers whether each signature is valid and whether every required signer has signed. To prove it is your document, hash it with Blake2b-256 and compare it against the hash in the response.
verifyOpen.officialHint: The genuine brand resource per network. A signing collection is only authentic if its metadata references one of these addresses. Confirm the address before trusting a collection.
verifyOpen.officialExplorer: View the resource in the explorer

anatomy.label: Anatomy of the seal
anatomy.h2b: the collection and its NFTs work
anatomy.sub: The whole Radix Seal model rests on two base NFTs you mint once, plus five NFT types kept inside your collection. Here is what each one is, who mints it and what it proves, made clear without jargon.
anatomy.foundationsTitle: The two base NFTs (one time only)

foundations.name: Seal NFT
foundations.role: It is your signer identity and the only key able to mint into your collection. You get it once from the official Radix Seal resource.
props: Soulbound: cannot be sold, moved or burned
Only you control it, bound to your account
Without it, nobody (not even this site) can create anything in your name

foundations.name: Signing collection
foundations.role: Your personal, reusable resource where every NFT you issue or sign is stored, numbered. Its owner rule is locked and requires your Seal.
props: Reusable: each document adds a numbered NFT (#1, #2, #3...)
Rules locked at creation: data unalterable forever
Only your Seal can mint into it, so nobody else can create signatures or invitations in your name

anatomy.typesTitle: The five NFT types inside the collection
anatomy.typesSub: They all share the same unforgeable chain of custody: they live in a collection owned by your soulbound Seal, in your account. That is why nobody can forge them in your name.

types.name: Signature invitation
types.mintedBy: Minted by whoever requests signatures, one per signer
types.proves: Public record of who was asked to sign that document
types.desc: Deposited into each signer's wallet. It carries the document hash and the invited account. It is a notice, not a signature; the issuer can recall it after a mistake, but can never touch a signature.

types.name: Signature
types.mintedBy: Minted by each signer into their own collection
types.proves: The account signed that specific document
types.desc: This is the record that truly counts as a signature: non-transferable, data locked. Impossible to forge because only the signer's Seal can mint into their collection.

types.name: Encryption signature
types.mintedBy: Minted by whoever encrypts, into their own collection
types.proves: The account encrypted that specific file
types.desc: Only in ROLA + Ledger mode. Always minted, with or without receivers: a public, permanent record in the encryptor's collection that this account encrypted the file, the encryption counterpart of a document signature.

types.name: Encryption invitation
types.mintedBy: Minted by whoever encrypts, one per authorized receiver
types.proves: The account is allowed to request decryption
types.desc: Only in ROLA + Ledger mode. Deposited into the receiver's wallet, carrying the encrypted file's hash. Without this invitation, an account cannot even request the key from the sender.

types.name: Decryption receipt
types.mintedBy: Minted by the receiver after obtaining the key
types.desc: Optional, in ROLA + Ledger mode. A public, permanent record in the receiver's collection that they obtained the key, verifiable by the sender on the ledger.

anatomy.note: All of this is public and permanent on the Radix Network. Anyone can read and verify it without depending on this site, with no account and no proprietary formats.

seal.title: Radix Seal | Self-Custody Document Signing, Encryption & Secure Chat
seal.description: Radix Seal is an open, self-custody trust standard on the Radix ledger: sign documents, encrypt files and chat with wallet-verified identities. No servers hold your files or keys; proofs are anchored on a public ledger anyone can verify.
